extracted.intended_audience: EPA decisionmakers, administrative law practitioners, environmental NGOs and counsel, regulatory analysts
extracted.subtask_short: petition for reconsideration of EPA rule
extracted.subtask_description: A legal petition asking EPA to convene reconsideration of specified aspects of a Final Rule (rescission of the Endangerment Finding and related vehicle GHG standards), challenging the agency's analytic choices, new de minimis test, and failure to quantify benefits. Focus is on procedural and substantive administrative-law and technical standards the Agency must meet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal sensitivity / avoidance of cherry-picking time windows
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of the ten-year period from 2016-25 cannot be treated as dispositive; the Agency must demonstrate that claimed variability (and alleged futility) exists 'not only in a single arbitrarily cherrypicked timeline but across a wide range of reasonable periods.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency should 'elaborate on the sensitivity of the variability figure to these temporal parameters' and show results across multiple reasonable periods; because climate change is a long-term cumulative phenomenon, short-term windows (e.g., annual data in 2016–2025) are inappropriate alone to conclude futility. The petitioners note the 2016–2025 window 'biases variability upwards' because it coincides with historically high GHG concentrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of longer-term averages to assess climate trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists often use temperature data averaged over longer time periods than one year to discern long-term climate change distinct from short-term natural variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer-term assessments (e.g., 10-year averages, multi-decade spans such as 1965–2025) are necessary because 'annual temperatures tell us what the atmosphere is doing right now' while longer averages let scientists detect permanent changes due to GHG accumulation. The petitioners illustrate that 10-year averaging materially reduces measured variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat climate-system regime changes as mere natural variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Elevated variability observed in a recent window (2016–2025) may reflect an altered climate regime caused by higher GHG concentrations, not only natural internal variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must avoid circular reasoning where variability caused by emissions is used to argue emissions regulation is futile: 'the elevated variability during the 2016-2025 window ... is at least partly a reflection of the altered climate state produced by the very GHG emissions whose regulation EPA now claims are meaningless.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use population standard deviation when the full set of years is observed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the temperature data for each year in a period (e.g., 2016–2025) are known (the entire 'population' of years), the Agency should use population standard deviation rather than sample standard deviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying the sample standard deviation in this context is 'statistically unsound.' If agency actually intended to treat the data as a sample drawn from a larger period, it must choose a random sample and justify that approach; arbitrary selection of 2016–2025 is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability and measurability statistics must be correctly calculated and justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics of variability and measurement uncertainty must be computed using appropriate averaging periods, statistical measures, and datasets, and those computations must be defensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners demonstrate that addressing flaws (accounting for CO2 relationship, using 10-year averages from 1965–2025, and using population SD) yields variability as low as 0.0193 °C—much lower than EPA's reported 0.14 °C. Measurement uncertainty examples: temperature measurement uncertainty of 0.02 °C (EPA dataset) and sea-level measurement uncertainty of 0.4 cm (NASA dataset).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparisons of modeled impacts to variability/measurability must account for compounding analytic choices
rubrics_metrics.description: When model choices depress impacts and metric choices inflate variability/measurability, these compounding errors must be addressed; corrected comparisons may show impacts far exceed EPA's comparators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners show that correcting both modeling and metric flaws produces much larger temperature and sea-level impacts (e.g., 0.115 °C in 2200 under one scenario, 0.269 °C under another) that exceed measurability and variability by orders of magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurability is not dispositive of meaningfulness; small quantified changes can be meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: An impact being within measurement sensitivity does not automatically render it meaningless for regulatory purposes; prior EPA determinations found even small modeled changes to be meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's earlier rules (e.g., 2010 light-duty GHG rule) treated global mean temperature reductions of 0.006–0.015 °C and sea-level changes of 0.06–0.14 cm as meaningful. Agency must reconcile its new focus on measurability with prior findings and explain any change in position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must reconcile new metrics with prior determinations and explain departures
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Agency adopts new comparative metrics or a new interpretation that contradicts prior findings, it must acknowledge the change and provide a reasoned explanation for departing from prior practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to address the reasoning of earlier rules renders the departure 'procedurally unexplained and substantively wrong.' The Agency must 'display awareness that it is changing position' and justify why prior conclusions that smaller impacts were meaningful are no longer applicable (citing FCC v. Fox).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-and-comment requirement for novel de minimis thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency proposing to adopt a specific de minimis threshold (e.g., 1%) must provide notice of that threshold in the proposal so the public can comment; adoption of a novel threshold in the final rule without notice deprives the public of a meaningful opportunity to comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners argue the Final Rule's introduction of a 1% test (not mentioned in the proposal) was unforeseeable and therefore subject to mandatory reconsideration under administrative procedure principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency bears the burden to show a de minimis threshold is appropriate in context
rubrics_metrics.description: General de minimis doctrine requires a case-specific showing; whether an amount is 'truly de minimis' depends on particular circumstances and the Agency must follow a rational approach to determine what level is de minimis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: Alabama Power Co. v. Costle; Pub. Citizen v. Young. The Agency cannot adopt a blanket 1% rule without showing that it weeds out 'truly de minimis' emissions in the context at issue and cannot use de minimis to 'thwart a statutory command.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent must be applied in context; thresholds are not portable across statutory schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases that use numerical thresholds (including a 1% screen) arose in different statutory contexts with different analytical records; such thresholds do not automatically support adoption in other contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: EME Homer City's 1% screening in the interstate transport context (CAA §110(a)(2)(D)(i)) was part of a specific analytic regime and cannot be transplanted to §202(a) regulation of mobile-source GHGs without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical justification required when adopting screening or de minimis thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Agency uses a numeric screen (e.g., 1%), it must provide technical analyses supporting the selection of that threshold in the relevant regulatory context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Transport Rule included substantial technical analysis to justify 1% as an efficient screening threshold; the Final Rule provided 'no technical justification whatsoever' for using 1% to declare regulation futile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrality of thresholds to the rule requires heightened procedural care
rubrics_metrics.description: If a threshold (such as 1%) is a dispositive basis for rescinding core findings (e.g., the Endangerment Finding), the Agency's adoption of that threshold is of 'central relevance' and must be subject to adequate notice, explanation, and opportunity for comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because EPA's futility rationale and repeal of the Endangerment Finding rely on the 1% test, mandatory reconsideration is required where the threshold was introduced without notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must acknowledge and explain departures from long-standing economic analysis guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Agency declines to monetize health benefits contrary to its Guidelines for Preparing Economic Analyses and prior practice, it must acknowledge the change and provide a detailed reasoned justification addressing the specific facets of the Guidelines being abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's Guidelines (peer-reviewed) and Executive Order 12,866 require quantifying health benefits to the fullest extent possible; a brief, unexplained refusal to monetize (citing unspecified 'analytical uncertainties') is inadequate. The Agency must disclose each aspect of its Guidelines it is departing from and explain why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization of health benefits should not be zeroed out based on generic assertions of uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Wholesale failure to quantify or monetize health benefits (e.g., ozone and PM2.5 reductions) because of 'analytical uncertainties' is unreasonable and skews cost–benefit comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must either monetize benefits using existing vetted approaches (with uncertainty characterization) or explain why quantification is impossible; prior practice and case law (e.g., Ctr. for Biological Diversity v. NHTSA) show refusal to quantify can be arbitrary when benefits are likely nonzero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vetted scientific and advisory-reviewed methodologies for health impact assessment unless explicitly justified
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's prior methods—Integrated Scientific Assessments, Technical Support Documents, Science Advisory Board and CASAC reviews, and its economic Guidelines—are well-vetted; departing from them requires explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Rule must explain why 'this well-vetted and transparent approach now fails to pass muster' rather than simply discarding quantified benefit estimates; improvements can be made over time but wholesale abandonment requires reasoned justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural reconsideration required where novel, central positions were not subject to public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Final Rule adopts novel, central positions (e.g., 1% de minimis test; refusal to monetize health benefits) that were not presented in the proposal, affected parties are entitled to reconsideration under Clean Air Act section 307(d)(7)(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because it was impracticable to raise objections when the novel positions were not in the proposal and those positions are central to rescission of the Endangerment Finding, EPA is required to grant reconsideration on those issues.
